title: Odd Count Minus Even Count
statement:
You get a lowercase string s. Pick two letters that occur in s: a letter x that occurs an odd number of times and a letter y that occurs an even number of times.

Return the largest possible value of count(x) − count(y). The input always contains at least one letter with an odd count and at least one with an even count. The answer may be negative.

examples.why: Counts: a 3, b 2, c 5, d 1. Take the largest odd count (c, 5) minus the smallest even count (b, 2).
x occurs 4 times, which is even, so it cannot be the odd letter. The best is z (1) minus y (2).
n has the largest count, 6, but it is even. Among even counts the smallest, o with 2, is the one to subtract: 3 − 2.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
At least one letter has an odd count and at least one has a positive even count
hints: The two letters are chosen independently. How do you maximise a difference a − b when a and b come from separate pools?
Make a as large as possible and b as small as possible.
Count every letter, then take the largest odd count and the smallest even count among the letters that actually occur.

explain.intuition:
The choice of the odd letter does not limit the choice of the even letter, so the best difference is simply the largest odd count minus the smallest even count. Count the 26 letters once and scan the counts.

The trap is letters with count 0. Zero is even, but a letter that does not appear cannot be picked. Skip zero counts, or the answer would always be just the largest odd count.
steps: For each count c > 0: if odd, update maxOdd; if even, update minEven.
pitfalls: Treating missing letters as count 0, which is even. That makes minEven always 0.
Using the overall largest count minus the overall smallest. The largest count may be even, as in the second example.

solutions.title: Try every pair of letters
solutions.idea: Count letters, then test every (odd letter, even letter) pair and keep the best difference.

solutions.title: Largest odd minus smallest even
solutions.idea: The two picks are independent, so maximise the odd count and minimise the even count separately.

followups: Ask the same question for every substring of length at least k and return the best. Why does that become much harder?
